subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Event Horizon
description: Learn The Event Horizon in one minute.

hook.text: The event horizon is the point of no return. Cross it, and nothing can ever come back—not even information.

buildup.text: It's not a physical surface—just a boundary in space. You wouldn't feel anything special as you crossed it.

discovery.text: Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations in 1916 and found this boundary. He was in a WWI trench at the time.

twist.text: From outside, you'd see someone falling in slow down and fade—frozen at the horizon by time dilation.

climax.text: The event horizon isn't the black hole itself. It's just the last place light can still escape.

punchline.text: A one-way door in spacetime. Enter, and the universe forgets you.

quiz.question: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
options: The boundary beyond which nothing can escape, not even light
The solid surface of the collapsed star
The point where the singularity begins to form

details.summary: The event horizon is the invisible boundary around a black hole beyond which escape is impossible. It's not a physical surface but a point of no return defined by gravity. Once anything — light, matter, information — crosses this threshold, it is permanently cut off from the rest of the universe.
details.whyItMatters: The event horizon defines what makes a black hole a black hole. It is the boundary where known physics breaks down, making it one of the most profound concepts in general relativity.
takeaways: The event horizon is a point of no return, not a surface
Nothing that crosses it can ever escape or communicate out
Its radius depends on the black hole's mass

faq.question: Can you see the event horizon?
faq.answer: Not directly — it emits nothing. But the Event Horizon Telescope captured the shadow of a black hole silhouetted against its glowing accretion disk. The dark region in the M87 image corresponds to the area inside and near the event horizon.

faq.question: How big is an event horizon?
faq.answer: It scales linearly with mass. A 10-solar-mass black hole has an event horizon about 60 km across. The supermassive black hole in M87 has an event horizon larger than our entire solar system. Earth compressed into a black hole would have a horizon roughly 18 mm across.
